## A short introduction 

Our goal here is to get a first draft of the Crepidostomum genome. To do this, we have different types of
data that we have previously processed:

   - Nanopore Minion. We have done the basecalling: Ex68_3

   - PacBio. Confused data: take a good look at it. According to Isa, she also got hold of two individuals
            of Crepidostomum, but they are not the same as those of Nanopore. And they are not parasites
            of Coregonus, but of Arctic charr.


   - Illumina Shot Gun. Two compressed .fastq.gz files for Crepidostomum. A single individual: Ex71_6.


As for mount options, I have mainly two

2. Do two genome drafts: first with the Nanopore MinIon data and then with the PacBio data. In this way 
we could determine which are the data that present a better coverage and use them as a "base".
3. Make a single genome draft with all the data, without distinction by individual. This is made possible
by flye's option to collapse the similar regions of haplotypes. Less optimal due to the loss of quality
or accuracy of the genome draft.

So, first of all, flye is executed with the nanopore and pacbio rawdata, that is, to make a hybrid
assembly of both types of long sequences. I will take the PacBio data as base first, and next, Nanopore data as base. Finally, a polish is done with the Illumina data.

# Assembly with FLYE

### Hybrid assembly with both PacBio and Nanopore 

NOTE: flye: error: argument --pacbio-hifi: not allowed with argument --nano-hq
Flye does not acceot the two arguments in the same run. Lucky for us, the author
resolved this issue in his Github:
https://github.com/fenderglass/Flye/issues/98

```{bash}
## Solution from the author in GitHub

#flye --pacbio-raw $PBREADS $ONTREADS --iterations 0 --out-dir $OUTPUTDIR  --genome-size 3.5g --threads $THREADS
#flye --pacbio-raw $PBREADS --resume-from polishing --out-dir $OUTPUTDIR  --genome-size 3.5g --threads $THREADS
```

```{bash}
if [ ! -d flye ]; then mkdir flye; fi

NANO="../2023-04-19/CRP/*.fastq"
PACBIO="../../data/PacBio/fastqs/demultiplex.bc1018_BAK8B_OA--bc1018_BAK8B_OA.hifi_reads.fastq.gz"

OUT="flye/PB_ONT"

if [ ! -d ./flye/PB_ONT ]; then
  flye --pacbio-raw $PACBIO $NANO -o $OUT -t 16 --iterations 0
  flye --pacbio-raw $PACBIO -o $OUT -t 16 --resume-from polishing
fi

OUT1="flye/ONT_PB"

if [ ! -d ./flye/ONT_PB ]; then
  flye --nano-raw $NANO $PACBIO -o $OUT1 -t 16 --iterations 0
  flye --nano-raw $NANO -o $OUT1 -t 16 --resume-from polishing
fi

```

## Assess draft genome quality (BUSCO)

We are going to asses the quality of the draft genomes, first for --pacbio-raw option as base and the other for 
--nano-raw option as base.

lineage that Jeremy uses: metazoa_odb10


```{bash }
DRAFT='flye/PB_ONT/assembly.fasta'

if [ ! -d pacbio ]; then
  busco -i $DRAFT -l metazoa_odb10 -o pacbio -m genome --cpu 16
fi

DRAFT1='flye/ONT_PB/assembly.fasta'
if [ ! -d nano ]; then
  .busco -i $DRAFT1 -l metazoa_odb10 -o nano -m genome --cpu 16
fi
```

## Summaries
### Distribution of contig lengths

```{r summaries}
nanoAssembly <- read.table('flye/ONT_PB/assembly_info.txt',
                           col.names = c('contig', 'length', 'cov', 'circ',
                                         'repeat', 'mult', 'skip', 'skip'),
                           colClasses = c('character', 'numeric', 'numeric',
                                          'factor', 'factor', 'numeric',
                                          'NULL', 'NULL'))
pacbioAssembly <- read.table('flye/PB_ONT/assembly_info.txt',
                             col.names = c('contig', 'length', 'cov', 'circ',
                                           'repeat', 'mult', 'skip', 'skip'),
                             colClasses = c('character', 'numeric', 'numeric',
                                            'factor', 'factor', 'numeric',
                                            'NULL', 'NULL'))
stopifnot(! is.unsorted(rev(pacbioAssembly$length)))
stopifnot(! is.unsorted(rev(nanoAssembly$length)))
nanoAssembly$sum <- cumsum(nanoAssembly$length)
pacbioAssembly$sum <- cumsum(pacbioAssembly$length)
nanoSize <- sum(pacbioAssembly$length)
pacbioSize <- sum(pacbioAssembly$length)
nanoN50  <- which(nanoAssembly$sum >= 0.5 * nanoSize)[1]
pacbioN50 <- which(pacbioAssembly$sum >= 0.5 * pacbioSize)[1]
barplot(nanoAssembly$length, col = 'gray', border = 'gray',
        xlim = c(1,7000), ylim = c(0, 250000),
        xlab = 'Ordered contigs', ylab = 'Contig length (bp)')
abline(v = nanoN50, col = 'red', lty = 2)
par(new = TRUE)
barplot(pacbioAssembly$length, col = 'black', axes = FALSE,
        xlim = c(1,7000), ylim = c(0, 250000),)
abline(v = pacbioN50, col = 'green', lty = 2)
```

The decreasingly ordered lengths of contigs of both assemblies suggest that the
assembly made with Oxford Nanopore data (in gray above) is much better: contigs
and total assembly length are much longer than in the PacBio assembly.

### *Peaks* of coverage depth

```{r peakdepth}
plot(density(nanoAssembly$cov), xlim = c(0, 30), col = 'darkred',
     main = 'Density of mean coverage per contig',
     xlab = 'Mean coverage', ylab = 'Density')
lines(density(pacbioAssembly$cov), col = 'darkgreen')
legend('topright', col = c('darkred','darkgreen'), lty=1,
       legend = c('Oxford Nanopore', 'PacBio'))
```

Both assemblies show two peaks of coverage depth, at almost 5 and at almost 20.
Approximately 34% of contigs, but less than 15% of the assembly length, seem
to be represented over 4 times more than most of the genome. A factor of 4 in
coverage differences among genome portions does not have an obvious explanation.
The *octoploid* fraction has a slightly higher GC content (not shown), possibly
indicating a different nature (just "repetitive") of those sequences. But, the
overlap in GC content distributions of the two genomic components is large. By
the way, @Petkeviciute2008 shows a species of *Crepidostomum* has 6 pairs of
chromosomes ($n=6$).

Contigs with a mean coverage higher than 25 should probably be excluded from
any analysis.

### BUSCO analysis

```{r removable}
write.table(nanoAssembly[nanoAssembly$cov > 25, 'contig'],
            file = 'overcovered_contigs.txt', row.names = FALSE,
            col.names = FALSE, quote=FALSE)
```

```{r moreSummary}
library('jsonlite')
library('MetBrewer')
  nano <- fromJSON('nano/short_summary.specific.metazoa_odb10.nano.json')
pacbio <- fromJSON('pacbio/short_summary.specific.metazoa_odb10.pacbio.json')
busco  <- as.matrix(data.frame(
  OxfordNanopore = c(nano$results$Missing,
                     nano$results$Fragmented,
                     nano$results$'Multi copy',
                     nano$results$'Single copy'),
  PacBio = c(pacbio$results$Missing,
             pacbio$results$Fragmented,
             pacbio$results$'Multi copy',
             pacbio$results$'Single copy')
))
rownames(busco) <- c('Missing', 'Fragmented', 'Multi-copy', 'Single-copy')
pal <- met.brewer(name = 'Tam', n = 4, type = 'discrete')
barplot(busco, col = pal, border = pal)
legend('bottomright', fill = pal,
       legend = c('Missing', 'Fragmented', 'Multi-copy', 'Single-copy'))
```

BUSCO results confirm that the assembly made with Oxford Nanopore data
first is a little better, in that at least a few of the expected genes were
detected, either as single-copy or fragmented.
